judgments.catchwords: whether a debt financing agreement in the form of a “whole turnover agreement”, had breached s 5(1) of the Moneylenders Act 1951 (MA). A whole turnover agreement between a financier (X) and borrower (Y) provides for - (1) X to advance money to Y with Y’s assignment to X of all of Y’s “future receivables” or Y’s future book debts (Y’s Assignment); and (2) Y’s Assignment shall take effect on a date stated in the whole turnover agreement which is - (a) before Y has issued any invoice to Y’s debtor(s); (b) before Y’s receivables are due to be paid to Y; and (c) before any debt has accrued in favour of Y and is payable to Y. A whole turnover agreement is also known as a “receivables purchase agreement”, “whole turnover factoring” and “whole turnover invoice discounting”.

judgments.title: Long Ding Jung v Leet Entertainment Sdn. Bhd.
judgments.catchwords: Winding-Up Petition – formal legal application made to the High Court asking for a company to be compulsory dissolved – Initiated by a former CEO seeking to wind up the respondent company over unpaid remuneration – Inability to Pay Debts – The statutory ground under Section 465(1)(e) of the Companies Act 2016 – Allows a court to wind up a company – Company is no longer able to meet its current financial liabilities as they fall due – Whether a petitioner must obtain a civil court judgment before serving a statutory notice of demand and presenting a winding-up petition. Statutory Notice of Demand (Section 466(1)(a) Companies Act 2016) – A mandatory 21-day legal notice served at a company's registered office requiring payment of a debt – The company fails to pay, secure, or compound the sum within 21 days – Triggers a statutory presumption that the company is unable to pay its debts. Commercial Insolvency – Whether a company's undisputed state of net current liabilities overrides a dispute over a petitioner's debt – A state where a company's balance sheet reflects severe financial distress – Court noted that while commercial insolvency was evident, it does not give a petitioner immediate standing if their specific debt is disputed. Bona Fide Dispute on Substantial Grounds – Whether the underlying debt for salary arrears was genuinely and objectively disputed by the respondent – The core legal test used to defeat a winding-up petition – A dispute must be honest (bona fide) and backed by objective, documented facts (substantial grounds) rather than just bare denials – The shifting claim amounts and unresolved transactions created a substantial dispute. Debt Recovery Substitution – A principle of equity stating that winding-up proceedings must not be abused as a shortcut for ordinary debt collection – If a debt is genuinely contested, a creditor must file a standard civil lawsuit instead of using the heavy-handed threat of winding up a company. Conflicting Affidavit Evidence – Written sworn statements by opposing parties that directly contradict each other on crucial facts – Whether third-party payments were salary advances or cash-flow help – Cannot be resolved on paper and require a full trial with oral cross-examination. Locus Standi (Standing) – The legal right of a party to bring a specific claim or demand before a court – Whether a petitioner has the legal standing to personally demand outstanding Employees Provident Fund (EPF) contributions in a standard corporate statutory demand notice – Petitioner lacked locus standi to personally demand or sue for outstanding EPF contributions, as that right belongs exclusively to a different entity. Separate Corporate Personality – The legal doctrine (Salomon v Salomon) that a company is a distinct legal entity separate from its shareholders or sister companies. Severability of Statutory Demand – Whether a court can "cut out" an invalid part of a statutory demand notice and let the valid part stand.

judgments.catchwords: The Plaintiff, a wound-up company suing through its court-appointed liquidator, alleged a conspiracy to defraud it via a sham management agreement over a palm oil estate. Several Defendants sought security for costs under s. 580A of the Companies Act 2016. The Court held the threshold satisfied — the Plaintiff's liquidation, an unpaid costs order and the absence of any contributory able to assist being credible testimony of inability to pay. The burden having shifted, the Plaintiff discharged it: its impecuniosity was materially contributed to by the very Defendants seeking security, the liquidator performs a public function, and the sums sought would stifle a genuine claim. Applications dismissed with costs. CIVIL PROCEDURE: Security for costs — Company in liquidation — Credible testimony of inability to pay — Shifting of burden — Impecuniosity caused by defendants seeking security — Whether oppressive — Companies Act 2016, s. 580A — Rules of Court 2012, O. 23 r. 1 COMPANY LAW: Winding up — Court-appointed liquidator performing public function — Conspiracy and breach of fiduciary duty — Merits not examined at interlocutory stage

judgments.title: MAPLE AMALGAMATED SDN BHD (DALAM PENYELESAIAN) v LIM CHENG POW & ors

parties.label: DEFENDAN
names: LIEW HON KONG @ LIEW KWAN VOON
LEE SIAH SIAN @ LEE HAY HIAN

judgments.catchwords: The plaintiff, a company in liquidation, applied under Order 22A of the Rules of Court 2012 for interim payment of RM36,828,330.00 against the 1st, 2nd and 12th defendants, arising out of a Management Agreement under which the 12th defendant managed the plaintiff's oil palm estate for a guaranteed monthly fee of RM100,000.00 but paid almost nothing. The Court held that no interim payment could rest on the plaintiff's primary case that the agreement was a sham, as allegations of conspiracy and fraud require cogent evidence to be tested at trial, and the quantum advanced was speculative and internally inconsistent. The alternative contractual claim, however, was made out: the agreement and the non-payment were undisputed, a unilateral proposal to reduce the fee met with silence was no variation where mutual written agreement was required, and the 12th defendant could not rely on the agreement while disclaiming its payment obligation. An earlier suit struck off without liberty to file afresh remained binding and confined the computation to fees accruing from July 2023, limitation having no operative effect on that period. The claim against the 1st and 2nd defendants personally failed, as they were not parties to the agreement and the concealment principle is a matter for trial. Interim payment of RM3,400,000.00 was accordingly ordered against the 12th defendant alone, payable within 30 days, subject to readjustment under Order 22A rule 8. CIVIL PROCEDURE: Interim payment — Order 22A r 3(1)(c), Rules of Court 2012 — Whether plaintiff would obtain judgment for substantial damages at trial — Suitability where sham and conspiracy alleged — Quantum and discretion — Issue estoppel from earlier striking out — Relief raised only in submissions CONTRACT: Variation — Requirement of mutual written agreement — Proposal met with silence — Approbation and reprobation COMPANY LAW: Separate legal personality — Personal liability of directors — Concealment principle LIMITATION: Periodic payments — Section 6(1)(a), Limitation Act 1953
judgments.judge: YA Puan Arziah binti Mohamed Apandi
